info.bio:
Toto es una banda estadounidense de Blues, Rock, Pop, Jazz, Funk, pero sus tres estilos musicales principales son el rock, funk y pop, Toto tuvo un notable éxito comercial en la decada de 1980. Es muy conocido por la habilidad para combinar diferentes estilos musicales; como los ya mencionados. La banda ha realizado a la fecha 17 álbumes y ha vendido cerca de 30 millones de copias.

El grupo musical Toto se formó en Los Ángeles en el año 1977

scenes.name: Techno-rock y pop de estudio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El «sonido» por encima de la melodía, el ritmo y la armonía: Electric Light Orchestra inventa el «high-tech pop»; Supertramp, Alan Parsons Project, Kansas, Styx y Split Enz. El valor de la producción define a Steely Dan (el pop-jazz pulido de los yuppies), Hall & Oates, los Fleetwood Mac de Rumours y Tusk, Toto, el «muro de sonido» titánico de Jim Steinman (Bat Out Of Hell) y la Penguin Cafe Orchestra. A finales de los setenta, el art-rock culmina en los supergrupos: 10cc, Godley & Creme, Foreigner, UK, Asia, Sky.

podcast.title: Shared Tour with The Ramones (January 26, 1979)
podcast.body: In a bizarre pairing reflecting major labels' misunderstanding of punk, The Ramones were chosen to open shows for Toto on a tour. A notable instance occurred on January 26, 1979, in Lake Charles, Louisiana, where the bill also included Foreigner and Blue Oyster Cult. "the Ramones were picked to open shows for Toto."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Steve Lukather's Guitar Solo (1981)
podcast.body: Steve Lukather of Toto contributed a "scorching guitar solo" to Olivia Newton-John's hit song "Physical," which was highlighted as one of the elements contributing to its massive success. "It has a scorching guitar solo courtesy of Steve Lucat there from Toto."

podcast.title: Grammy Win Controversy (1983)
podcast.body: Toto's wins for "Toto IV" (Album of the Year) and "Rosanna" (Record of the Year) at the 1983 Grammys were highly controversial among 1980s rock critics, who cited them as evidence of the Recording Academy's "out of touchness." Despite the criticism, the album was popular, achieving triple platinum status and producing major hits. "If you read The Rock Press during the 1980s, in any piece critiquing the Grammys, and there were many, Christopher Cross's sweep and Toto's wins were exhibits A and B of the recording academies out of touchness."

podcast.title: Reaction to Weezer's "Africa" Cover (2018)
podcast.body: The original band Toto was "absolutely thrilled" about Mary Klym's campaign and Weezer's subsequent cover of "Africa." Steve Lukather even sent Mary Klym a video message, with Ringo Starr humorously "cooking around" in the background. "And total, the original band behind the song, is absolutely thrilled about what Mary Clem of Cleveland did for the song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration on "Beat It"
podcast.body: Three members of Toto contributed to Michael Jackson's song "Beat It," with Steve Lukather specifically playing the main guitar riff. "In fact, three members of Toto play on Michael Jackson's beat it."

podcast.title: High-Caliber Session Musicians
podcast.body: The band was comprised of some of the best session players in the world; for instance, guitarist Steve Lukather played the guitar on Michael Jackson's "Beat It" (excluding Eddie Van Halen's solo), and Jeff Porcaro was the drummer. "Totos was made up of some of the best session players in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Artists of Covered Songs
podcast.body: Toto are the original artists of the songs "Africa" (1982) and "Rosanna," both of which were covered by Weezer, largely due to fan requests. "Weezer's version of Africa, the total hit from 1982."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reputation as a "Corporate Rock Band"
podcast.body: Toto was known as a "corporate rock band," a term for projects intentionally designed to be mainstream and sell as many records as possible. This made them "highly uncool" to a segment of the rock audience, particularly the alt-rock crowd, who felt they were "not supposed to like Toto." "Toto was what we used to call a corporate rock band."
